name: Gravimetric Induction Pistol GIP-4 'Undertow'
description:
The Gravimetric Induction Pistol operates on a principle that remains proprietary to OUROBOROS ENERGY despite years of competitor reverse-engineering attempts: it generates a localized gravimetric anomaly at range by briefly inducing a controlled mass-energy fluctuation through a compact induction array derived from OUROBOROS's experimental power generation research. In practical terms, the weapon projects a field approximately 40 centimeters in diameter that, for a duration of 0.6 to 2.4 seconds, increases effective gravitational acceleration within that field to between 4G and 9G depending on charge level. Targets caught in the field experience sudden, extreme downward force — enough to collapse joints, fracture load-bearing bones, and rupture intervertebral discs at high settings. At low settings, it is sufficient to pin a standing target to the floor and prevent movement.

OUROBOROS ENERGY developed the induction array for entirely different purposes — specifically, for manipulating heavy industrial components in confined spaces where mechanical lifting equipment cannot operate. The weaponization of the technology was, by most accounts, accidental: an industrial incident in which a malfunctioning array pinned three workers to a catwalk for several minutes before losing power demonstrated the technology's potential in a way that OUROBOROS's defense applications division found difficult to ignore. The GIP-4 is the fourth iteration of the resulting weapon program, and the first to achieve a form factor small enough to be carried as a sidearm.

The Undertow has acquired a reputation for the specific, recognizable nature of the injuries it produces. Physicians who treat gravitational compression injuries can identify them immediately — the pattern of skeletal damage, the characteristic joint failures, the bruising geometry — and this has become a forensic liability for operators. In GLMZ, 'gravity bruising' is increasingly recognized by both law enforcement and insurance forensics, making the Undertow less useful for operators who require deniability. Those who don't require deniability, however, find it extraordinarily effective.
specifications:
effective range: 30m
field diameter: 40 cm at target
gravity multiplier: 4G–9G (4 settings)
field duration: 0.6–2.4 seconds (charge-dependent)
power source: OUROBOROS Induction Cell OIC-1 (8 shots at maximum charge, 24 at minimum)
weight: 2.3 kg
length: 28 cm
charge time: 2.1 seconds (maximum charge), 0.7 seconds (minimum charge)
field accuracy: ±12 cm at 30m
tactical_use: Operators typically use the Undertow to pin targets for secondary actions — restraint, extraction, or follow-up engagement — rather than as a primary damage tool. At maximum charge, it is used as a direct incapacitation or killing tool, particularly effective against targets in elevated positions where sudden gravitational increase causes falls. In confined spaces, operators use it to collapse targets through structural interference — pinning someone against a floor while a ceiling is low enough to cause additional compression injury. The weapon's limited shot count and charge time make it unsuitable as a primary weapon in sustained engagements.
cultural_context: The Undertow is genuinely rare — OUROBOROS ENERGY produces limited quantities and maintains strict distribution controls, partly for legal reasons and partly because the induction array components are expensive and difficult to manufacture. Possessing one is a statement of access as much as intent. In GLMZ's criminal ecology, the Undertow is associated with high-end contract work — the kind of operator who carries one is assumed to be expensive, professional, and working for someone with significant resources. The forensic visibility of its injuries has made it a subject of interest in legal circles, where a push to establish 'gravimetric harm' as a distinct criminal category is slowly gaining traction.
known_users: OUROBOROS ENERGY internal security (rare, select units)
story_hooks: OUROBOROS ENERGY's induction cell supply chain has been quietly disrupted — someone is buying up OIC-1 cells before they reach distribution. GIP-4 units across the city are going dark. Someone wants all the Undertows offline simultaneously.

A forensic physician has published a paper identifying 'gravimetric harm' as a distinct injury classification and linking 11 deaths over three years to GIP-4 use. OUROBOROS's legal department has filed to suppress the paper. The physician has received the filing and is deciding what to do next.
An OUROBOROS industrial facility has reported a theft — not of weapons, but of induction array components. Enough to build several GIP-4 equivalents. Someone is manufacturing unauthorized units.

A high-profile political figure was found dead with injuries consistent with gravitational compression, but no GIP-4 was recovered and no OUROBOROS cells were detected in the environment. Either someone cleaned up perfectly or the technology has been replicated in a form OUROBOROS doesn't recognize.

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact, angular pistol with an unusually deep profile — the grip-to-muzzle ratio suggests internal complexity. The barrel appears shortened and slightly wider than conventional firearms, tapering into a distinctive cylindrical emitter head that dominates the front third of the weapon. The overall shape reads as 'aggressive geometry': sharp edges, pronounced angles, no curves except where function demands them.
physical_description.dimensions: Length: 28 cm | Grip depth: 5.2 cm | Emitter head diameter: 4.1 cm | Barrel effective length: 8 cm
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and front-heavy — the 2.3 kg mass concentrates forward in the induction array housing, giving the weapon a pronounced muzzle-down bias. Requires deliberate wrist support; not a weapon for one-handed sustained aim.
physical_description.primary_material: Aerospace-grade polymer composite frame with embedded ferrous stabilization ribs. Internal structure visible through semi-translucent panels on slide showing layered induction coils. Muzzle emitter is hardened steel with visible thermal scoring.
physical_description.finish: Matte gunmetal polymer with brushed steel accents. The induction head displays characteristic scorch marks and mineral discoloration from repeated mass-energy cycling — faint rainbow oxidation patterns around the emitter aperture. Wear concentrated on grip and charging mechanism from field use.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary: dark gunmetal gray (polymer body) | Accents: brushed steel (emitter, charging lever, sight rails) | Highlights: faint iridescent heat-stress coloration (purple, amber) around the muzzle from energy discharge
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured polymer with knurled grip panels — aggressive checkering pattern designed for gloved operation. The charging lever is wrapped in thin rubberized material, worn smooth from repeated cycling. The trigger guard is sharp-edged and feels intentionally hostile.
distinctive_features: Recessed induction array visible as concentric rings through semi-opaque polymer panel on slide
Two prominent heat vents (upper/lower receiver) with visible internal ribbing for thermal dissipation
Unconventional charging mechanism — a side-mounted lever with detents indicating four discrete power settings
Cylindrical emitter head features three small alignment ports arranged in a triangular pattern (targeting system calibration points)
OUROBOROS logo etched into slide — a serpent consuming its tail, stylized with geometric precision
Serial plate mounted on frame showing manufacturing date and induction array generation (OIC-1 specification)
Faint scorch marks radiating from the emitter aperture — evidence of repeated field use
Deep wear grooves in the grip from organic oil absorption despite polymer construction
A small red indicator dot on the charging lever — position indicates current power setting and charge status
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: OUROBOROS ENERGY corporate logo (Φ-stamped serpent motif) on left slide; serial plate mounted on lower receiver with alphanumeric identifier, manufacturing date, and OIC-1 power cell specification; small warning glyph (radiation-adjacent symbol denoting gravitational hazard) below the ejection port.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained but operationally weathered — no visible cracks or structural compromise, but surface shows consistent use: scuff marks on the grip, micro-scratches on the sight rails, accumulated polymer dust in the charging mechanism detents. The emitter head displays permanent thermal discoloration and mineral deposits from power cell residue. Kept functional but not pristine — field-operator aesthetic.
